item.title: Rogers seeks to offset hit from CRTC fee ban as wireless service revenue dips in Q3
item.description: Rogers Communications Inc. says it is seeking to offset the hit it has taken from the CRTC’s recent ban on telecommunications carriers charging certain administrative fees.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Rogers Communications Inc. says it is seeking to offset the hit it has taken from the CRTC’s recent ban on telecommunications carriers charging certain administrative fees. While Rogers reported a year-over-year increase in overall revenue during its most recent quarter, primarily due to growth in its media division, the company said wireless service revenue decreased one per cent. During its third quarter, Rogers’ mobile phone average monthly revenue per user was $55.22, down from $56.70 in the same quarter of the prior year. Chief financial officer Glenn Brandt said the “largest impact” to that closely watched figure came from the CRTC’s move in June to prohibit telecoms from charging customers when they activate, change or cancel plans. “The purpose of those setup fees was exactly that — to offset costs of account changes or new accounts coming on,” Brandt told analysts on a conference call Friday. “The charge disappeared (due to) the CRTC decision. The costs don’t.” He said Rogers put in place some “early initiatives” during the quarter to recover some of those costs, but “there’s still more work to do.” “We’re now moving back to finding alternatives for covering those costs, shipping costs, for example … so that effort remains ongoing.” The CRTC has said the new rules are meant to make it easier for customers to switch internet and cellphone plans without having to worry about unexpected charges. The regulator is in the midst of a review into whether Rogers, along with rivals Bell Canada and Telus Corp., violated the ban by introducing new fees around the time it took effect. It said Rogers began charging customers a $40 device setup fee, $25 shipping charge, and an unspecified SIM card fee in mid-June that “would not appear” to qualify for an exemption under the rules for optional services or products that consumers consent to purchase. Rogers has argued the device setup fee is related to an optional purchase. It also said the shipping and SIM fees were not new, and that the latter is only charged when a customer replaces a lost or damaged SIM, rather than at activation. Overall, the quarter saw a “less active telecom market,” said Rogers president and CEO Tony Staffieri said, as the company reported a profit attributable to shareholders of $482 million. “In wireless, we stayed focused on financials versus chasing subscriber volume in what is typically a busy back-to-school quarter,” he told analysts. The company reported 17,000 total mobile phone net subscriber additions, including 6,000 postpaid — those who pay a monthly bill for their wireless services after charges have accumulated. That was down from 62,000 postpaid additions in the same quarter last year. Rogers’ monthly churn — a measure of those who cancelled their service — for net postpaid mobile subscribers was 1.03 per cent, up from 0.99 per cent during its previous third quarter. Retail internet net additions totalled 10,000, down from 29,000 a year earlier. The company said its profit amounted to 88 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30. The result compared with a profit of $5.71 billion or $10.54 per diluted share a year ago when it saw a $5-billion non-cash gain related to its stake in Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment and $151-million gain on the redemption of long-term debt. On an adjusted basis, Rogers said it earned $704 million in net income, or $1.29 per diluted share in its latest quarter, down from an adjusted profit of $1.37 per diluted share a year ago. Revenue totalled $5.44 billion, up from $5.35 billion in the same quarter last year. “Financial results were in line with our forecast while subscriber growth was a little lighter than our forecast,” said RBC analyst Drew McReynolds in a note. “We view the results as largely neutral for the shares at current levels.” Earlier this month, Rogers completed its $4.35-billion purchase of the remaining 25 per cent stake in MLSE it did not already hold, giving it complete ownership of the sports conglomerate that includes the Maple Leafs, Raptors, Toronto FC and Argonauts. Staffieri reiterated Rogers’ plan to sell a minority interest in its consolidated sports, media and entertainment portfolio to third-party investors, adding he remains “bullish about our plan to unlock shareholder value and drive long-term growth.” Rogers is targeting the first half of 2027 to close that minority interest sale. “Investor interest in these assets is substantial as sports franchise valuations continue to rise,” Staffieri said. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026. By Sammy Hudes BNN Bloomberg, CTV News and CP24 are owned by Bell Media, which is a division of BCE.

item.title: Beyond big tech: 6 quality dividend stocks to own: Jon Erlichman
item.description: In Buchanan’s view, quality companies have steady, recurring revenue, pricing power, and enough cash to keep paying and raising dividends in good times and bad. Dividends, in his opinion, are a kind ...
item.content:encoded:
Quality is one of the most overused words in investing. But what makes a stock a quality stock? For Keith Buchanan, one clue is the dividend, and whether a company can keep paying it.

In the latest episode of Ticker Take , I spoke with Buchanan of GLOBALT Investments about how he uses that idea to find quality companies, which leads him to a number of opportunities beyond popular sectors like tech. In Buchanan’s view, quality companies have steady, recurring revenue, pricing power, and enough cash to keep paying and raising dividends in good times and bad. Dividends, in his opinion, are a kind of receipt that the business model is working. At the same time, Buchanan warns that high dividend yields can look like quality marks, when in fact they are the opposite. When a stock falls, its yield rises even if the company never pays an extra cent, so an unusually big yield can be the market warning you that the payout is in trouble. For that reason, Buchanan would rather own a company that can grow a smaller dividend than one that looks generous right before it has to cut. Here are six stocks he used to show how to assess quality companies. We have included some of the analyst recommendations, as measured by Bloomberg. As always, this is not financial advice. Delta Air Lines ( DAL ) Airlines have a rough history with investors: capital intensive, boom and bust, famous for adding too many seats at the wrong time. However, Buchanan says this cycle is different, with fewer and more global players showing real discipline. He says Delta in particular has been out front on a premium, loyalty-driven model, anchored by its American Express partnership. Delta cut its dividend during the pandemic, before bringing it back in 2023. He thinks the company can keep raising it. And he’s not alone in his bullishness. Nearly every analyst who covers the stock rates it a buy. Waste Management ( WM ) There is nothing glamorous about garbage, but trash leads to cash. Whether the economy grows or not, people and businesses keep producing waste, which gives Waste Management steady demand and real pricing power. Buchanan points to the recurring cash that has funded more than 20 straight years of dividend increases. About two-thirds of analysts rate it a buy. JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ) Wall Street is split on JPMorgan, with only about half of analysts calling it a buy, but that suits Buchanan just fine. He is willing to pay a premium for the biggest U.S. bank because of the cash the Chase franchise generates and the interest income he expects over the next few years. JPMorgan raised its dividend again this fall, and he says its commitment to that payout has held through every kind of cycle. Devon Energy ( DVN ) Energy is about as cyclical as it gets, and producers have little say over the prices they receive, so Buchanan focuses on the people running the company. He liked Devon’s merger with Coterra this year, which created a bigger producer with strong assets and a management team he trusts to ride out the swings and keep returning cash. Devon raised its dividend by roughly a third after the deal closed, and about nine out of every ten analysts rate it a buy. Hasbro ( HAS ) Hasbro’s dividend has been flat since 2022, so it would fail a strict dividend-growth screen, but Buchanan keeps it for where he thinks it is headed. The draw is the intellectual property, with franchises such as Magic: The Gathering offering better economics than traditional toys. Pair that with a solid balance sheet, he says, and Hasbro has the capacity to start growing its payout again. According to Bloomberg, more than 90 per cent of the street currently recommends the stock. Automatic Data Processing ( ADP ) ADP has raised its dividend for 50 years in a row, which is the longest streak on this list. While most analysts are not recommending the stock, it handles payroll for many leading businesses and throws off plenty of free cash flow. Buchanan notes it is not a direct AI winner, though it can use AI inside its own operations to widen margins. The Ticker Take Regardless of whether it’s an airline or a garbage business, Buchanan hunts for companies that generate cash and have the discipline to keep paying shareholders. That, to him, is the definition of quality. Jon Erlichman is a BNN Bloomberg contributor and the host of Ticker Take on YouTube . item.title: When should you start collecting CPP and OAS?: Stan Wong
item.description: Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP).
item.content:encoded:
Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP). Waiting until 70 rather than starting at 65 increases monthly payments by 42 per cent. The catch? Five years without collecting a penny.

Clients frequently ask me whether they should begin collecting CPP as early as age 60, wait until 65 or defer until 70, and when they should start Old Age Security (OAS). Many instinctively favour taking the money early. But the better question is how these decisions fit into their overall financial plan. Do you actually need the income? Consider two retirees, both aged 65. One has a workplace pension, substantial investments, and no immediate need for additional income. Deferring CPP could strengthen financial security later. The other relies on investment withdrawals to pay everyday expenses. Collecting earlier might reduce the need to sell investments during a market downturn. The same pension rules can produce very different answers. A comprehensive financial plan can project cash flow, compare investment withdrawals, and identify the trade-offs of waiting, including forgone returns and potential taxes. Taxes can change the calculation Both CPP and OAS are taxable, but only OAS faces an income-tested recovery tax, commonly called the clawback. For the 2026 income year, the OAS clawback starts above $95,323 in individual net income, with 15 cents recovered for each additional dollar. This generally affects recoveries from July 2027 through June 2028. At a net income of $120,000, including OAS, roughly $3,700 would be recovered. For recipients aged 65 to 74, the benefit can be fully clawed back at $155,320. CPP has no comparable clawback, although receiving it can increase taxable income and, consequently, OAS repayments. The broader retirement income picture is crucial: someone retiring before mandatory withdrawals from a registered retirement income fund (RRIF) begin may benefit from drawing down savings in a registered retirement savings plan (RRSP) during lower-income years while deferring benefits. Someone expecting substantial RRIF income later might face larger OAS clawbacks even after waiting. Coordinating pension income, registered account withdrawals and income-splitting opportunities can change which starting dates are most tax-efficient. The financial reward for waiting CPP can start at 60, with payments reduced by 36 per cent relative to 65. After 65, payments increase by 0.7 per cent for each month deferred, reaching 42 per cent at 70. OAS can start at 65. Waiting increases payments by 0.6 per cent monthly, or 36 per cent at 70. Neither benefit increases further for deferral beyond 70. Someone entitled to $1,000 monthly in CPP at 65 would receive $1,420 at 70, before future inflation adjustments. The maximum monthly OAS payment for aged 65 to 74 is $762.50 in late 2026. A 36 per cent increase would lift that base payment to approximately $1,037, before indexing. Both benefits are inflation-adjusted, and OAS rises automatically another 10 per cent at 75. How long must you live to come out ahead? Delaying $1,000 monthly in CPP from 65 to 70 means forgoing $60,000, then receiving an additional $420 monthly. On a simple cumulative-payment basis, the higher benefit catches up near age 82. For OAS, the comparable break-even is around age 83, accounting for the 10 per cent increase at 75 applicable to both starting ages. Taxes, inflation, and investment returns can change these results. According to the Office of the Chief Actuary’s 32nd CPP report , a Canadian man aged 65 in 2025 is projected to live another 21.6 years, reaching approximately age 87; for women, the projection is 24.1 years, reaching approximately age 89. These averages cannot predict individual outcomes. Health, lifestyle, and family history should inform longevity assumptions. For those who live into their 90s, higher inflation-adjusted benefits may reduce pressure on portfolios later in life. Individuals eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement should generally not defer OAS because doing so delays access to that supplement. A total wealth planning decision There is no universally correct age to begin CPP or OAS. Spouses may benefit from different starting dates, and taking one benefit earlier while deferring the other may make sense. Before deciding, Canadians should prepare or update a comprehensive financial plan that models different scenarios for income needs, tax exposure, portfolio sustainability, and estate objectives. The goal is not simply to collect sooner or secure the largest monthly cheque. It is to make these decisions within a broader total wealth plan that supports after-tax income and lasting financial security.
